AQA GCSE History 8145 · Conflict and Tension 1918–1939

Chapter 8 · The escalation
of tension

The Rhineland, Hitler’s alliances, Anschluss, the Sudeten Crisis, Munich and the debate over appeasement. Original interactive revision for Gabriel.

All written historical-source extracts appear as full typed text; images are retained for visual evidence, with their provenance and analysis alongside.

8.1
7 March 1936

The reoccupation of the Rhineland

Treaty breach and gamble

On 7 March 1936 Hitler sent about 22,000 German soldiers into the Rhineland, demilitarised under Versailles and protected by the Locarno settlement. The region was German territory; the treaty prohibited troops and fortifications there.

Why now?

The 1935 Franco-Soviet Pact gave Hitler a pretext: he claimed Germany was threatened from both east and west. Remilitarisation would protect the western frontier, making eastern expansion easier.

Why no military response?

France faced an election and was reluctant to act without Britain; its leaders exaggerated German strength. Britain was economically and militarily cautious, distracted by Abyssinia, and some believed Germany was merely entering its own territory. The League was occupied by the Abyssinian crisis.

Why a turning point?

Hitler ordered retreat if France resisted. The gamble succeeded and increased his confidence. Germany began fortifying its western frontier, while France felt less able to rely on Britain.

Source C · Lord Lothian, British politician, reacting in 1936
“After all, the Germans are only going into their own back garden.”

Analyse provenance / usefulness: A British view that minimised the breach; it does not represent every politician or prove the action was harmless.

Source D · Hitler reflecting on 1936
“If the French had taken any action we would have been easily defeated; our resistance would have been over in a few days.”

Analyse provenance / usefulness: Retrospective testimony reveals the risk, but Hitler had reasons to dramatise his boldness.

Source E · Winston Churchill speaking in the Commons, 26 March 1936
“The violation of the Rhineland is serious from the point of view of the menace to which it exposes Holland, Belgium, and France. When it is fortified it will be a barrier across Germany’s front door, which will leave her free to sally out eastward and southward by the back door.”

Analyse provenance / usefulness: Churchill warned about the strategic consequences of fortifying Germany’s western border.

Grade 8–9 exam skill: Explain the link between the event, the response of other powers and the consequence for the balance of power. For any source, consider its origin, audience, purpose and what contextual knowledge confirms or challenges it.
8.2
Alliances and diplomacy

Which countries supported Hitler?

Britain: sought, not secured

Hitler proposed a 25-year non-aggression agreement with Britain in 1936. Britain did not agree to a formal alliance. Avoid confusing appeasement, which tried to avert war, with joining Hitler.

Italy and the Rome–Berlin Axis

Mussolini opposed German interference in Austria in 1934, but the Abyssinian crisis damaged his relations with Britain and France. By October 1936 Italy and Germany had reached the Rome–Berlin Axis understanding.

Japan and the Anti-Comintern Pact

Germany and Japan signed the Anti-Comintern Pact in November 1936, publicly against international communism. Italy joined in 1937. These ties helped Germany overcome diplomatic isolation.

Spain: support for Franco

German and Italian forces assisted Francisco Franco in the Spanish Civil War. This allowed the Nazis to test weapons and tactics, support an anti-communist leader and gain experience, but Franco’s Spain was not formally an Axis member during the Second World War.

1939 Pact of Steel

Germany and Italy signed the Pact of Steel in May 1939: a much closer military-political commitment than the 1936 Axis understanding. Japan was not a signatory; the three powers signed a separate Tripartite Pact in 1940.

Grade 8–9 exam skill: Explain the link between the event, the response of other powers and the consequence for the balance of power. For any source, consider its origin, audience, purpose and what contextual knowledge confirms or challenges it.
8.3
12 March 1938

Anschluss with Austria, 1938

Why Austria?

Austria was Hitler’s birthplace and had German-speaking communities. Anschluss (union) was prohibited by Versailles and St Germain. Hitler wanted a Greater Germany, strategic access to south-eastern Europe and Austria’s resources and armed forces.

From failure to pressure

The failed 1934 Nazi coup and murder of Chancellor Dollfuss did not produce union, partly because Mussolini opposed it. By 1938 Italy was cooperating with Germany and unlikely to intervene.

Schuschnigg’s dilemma

Austrian Chancellor Kurt Schuschnigg faced Nazi demonstrations and coercive demands at Berchtesgaden in February 1938. He announced a plebiscite to defend Austrian independence. Hitler demanded its postponement and forced Schuschnigg to resign.

Seizure and vote

Arthur Seyss-Inquart became chancellor on 11 March. German troops entered Austria on 12 March without military resistance. A heavily controlled plebiscite in April reported about 99% support: it cannot be treated as an impartial measure of opinion.

Grade 8–9 exam skill: Explain the link between the event, the response of other powers and the consequence for the balance of power. For any source, consider its origin, audience, purpose and what contextual knowledge confirms or challenges it.
8.4
Different reactions, different experiences

How did people react to Anschluss?

Austria: celebration and persecution

Many Austrians welcomed the union with Germany, while others opposed it or feared the Nazis. Jewish Austrians immediately faced public humiliation, violence, persecution and threats. Visible cheering crowds are not evidence of universal approval.

Britain and France

Both governments were unwilling to fight over Austria. Many people viewed union of two German-speaking societies as understandable, even though it violated the treaties.

Czechoslovakia and the USSR

Czechoslovakia feared becoming Hitler’s next target; union put German power closer to its borders. The USSR was alarmed by German expansion and by the weakness of collective opposition.

Consequences

Hitler gained Austrian troops, raw materials and strategic access. Britain, France and the League did not reverse the annexation, strengthening his belief that further advances might go unchallenged.

Source B · Susi Seitz, an Austrian Hitler Youth leader, interviewed in 1997
“I just looked at him [Hitler] and I saw goodness. And in my heart I promised I will be faithful to you. And I kept that promise.”

Analyse provenance / usefulness: A recollection from decades later: revealing of this individual’s enthusiasm, not representative of every Austrian.

Grade 8–9 exam skill: Explain the link between the event, the response of other powers and the consequence for the balance of power. For any source, consider its origin, audience, purpose and what contextual knowledge confirms or challenges it.
8.5
September 1938

What was the Sudeten Crisis?

Why the Sudetenland mattered

The borderlands of Czechoslovakia included about three million ethnic Germans. The region also contained vital fortifications, transport routes and industries. Giving it up threatened Czechoslovakia’s defence.

Hitler’s claim and the real strategic prize

Hitler claimed Sudeten Germans needed protection and demanded self-determination. But taking the area also weakened an independent state that did not arise simply from Germany’s lost territory.

A crisis fuelled by pressure

Nazi activists and demonstrations encouraged instability. Hitler threatened force in 1938. British and French leaders feared a continental war and sought concessions.

Chamberlain’s negotiations

Chamberlain met Hitler at Berchtesgaden on 15 September, then at Bad Godesberg on 22 September. Hitler escalated his demands, pushing for rapid transfer of territory. Munich followed.

Source C · Hitler speaking to the people of Berlin in 1938
“We are not interested in breaking peace. I am thankful to Mr Chamberlain for all his trouble and I assured him that the German people want nothing but peace, but I also declared that I cannot go beyond the limits of our patience. I further assured him, and I repeat here, that if this problem is solved, there will be no further territorial problems in Europe for Germany.”

Analyse provenance / usefulness: Public speech intended to reassure an audience. Compare his assurance with the occupation of the rest of Czechoslovakia in March 1939.

Grade 8–9 exam skill: Explain the link between the event, the response of other powers and the consequence for the balance of power. For any source, consider its origin, audience, purpose and what contextual knowledge confirms or challenges it.
8.6
Munich, September 1938

Why was Chamberlain hopeful of “peace in our time”?

Munich Conference, 29–30 September 1938

Germany, Britain, France and Italy agreed to transfer the Sudetenland to Germany. Czechoslovakia was not represented at the negotiations; the USSR was excluded.

Chamberlain’s calculation

Chamberlain believed concessions could avoid an immediate war and that Hitler might be satisfied. In public he celebrated the Anglo-German declaration as a step towards peace.

The strategic cost

Losing the Sudetenland meant Czechoslovakia lost major defensive fortifications and important industries. Hitler had gained territory without war, and other powers had decided another state’s fate.

March 1939 broke the promise

In March 1939 Germany occupied the Czech lands of Bohemia and Moravia, going beyond claims to unite German speakers. The occupation discredited the claim that Hitler’s demands were limited. Britain subsequently guaranteed Polish independence.

Grade 8–9 exam skill: Explain the link between the event, the response of other powers and the consequence for the balance of power. For any source, consider its origin, audience, purpose and what contextual knowledge confirms or challenges it.
8.7
The pattern of appeasement

How did Britain and France react to Hitler’s actions?

A sequence of concessions

1933: Germany left the League and Disarmament Conference. 1935: rearmament, Saar plebiscite and the Anglo-German Naval Agreement. 1936: Rhineland remilitarised. 1938: Anschluss and Munich. 1939: occupation of Prague and a British guarantee to Poland.

Fear of another world war

The casualties and destruction of 1914–18 remained vivid. Many voters, particularly in Britain, wanted peace. Air attacks against cities seemed a terrifying prospect.

Weakness and division

The Depression strained budgets; Britain needed time to rearm and France faced domestic divisions. Some thought Versailles had been too harsh, and suspicion of Soviet communism sometimes made Hitler seem the lesser threat.

Did appeasement work?

It delayed war and allowed some rearmament, but also emboldened Hitler and weakened Czechoslovakia. A Grade 8–9 judgement must weigh what decision-makers knew then against what became clear later.

Grade 8–9 exam skill: Explain the link between the event, the response of other powers and the consequence for the balance of power. For any source, consider its origin, audience, purpose and what contextual knowledge confirms or challenges it.
8.8A
Evidence and contemporary reasoning

Was appeasement a good idea? · The case for

Peace was a major public demand

The First World War was still in living memory and the prospect of bombing terrified civilians. Chamberlain won genuine public support for his attempts to prevent another conflict.

Versailles seemed unfair

Some British observers thought German demands over the Rhineland and German-speaking communities addressed legitimate grievances. This perception encouraged concessions.

Britain needed time

British rearmament accelerated in the late 1930s. Negotiations could buy time to improve the armed forces, including air defence. However, Germany was also rearming.

Depression and isolation

Economic depression restricted the willingness to spend on war; the United States was pursuing neutrality. France depended heavily on British cooperation.

The case is not certainty

Defenders of appeasement argue it was reasonable under the circumstances, not that Hitler could be trusted or that the Munich settlement was fair to Czechoslovakia.

Source A · Daily Express, 30 September 1938
“People of Britain, your children are safe. Your husbands and sons will not march to battle. If we must have a victor let us choose Chamberlain. For the Prime Minister’s conquests are mighty and enduring – millions of happy homes and hearts relieved of their burden.”

Analyse provenance / usefulness: A contemporary pro-appeasement newspaper: helpful evidence of celebratory opinion, but it reflects editorial persuasion rather than proof of lasting peace.

Grade 8–9 exam skill: Explain the link between the event, the response of other powers and the consequence for the balance of power. For any source, consider its origin, audience, purpose and what contextual knowledge confirms or challenges it.
8.8B
Challenge and judgement

Was appeasement a good idea? · The case against

Misjudging Hitler

Critics argue policymakers overestimated Hitler’s willingness to keep promises, despite his stated expansionist aims and repeated treaty breaches.

Missed opportunities to stop him

German forces were weak when they entered the Rhineland in 1936. A firm response might have stopped remilitarisation, though this outcome is not certain.

Consequences for other states

Austria was annexed and Czechoslovakia was forced to yield its defences. Appeasement also damaged Soviet confidence in Britain and France.

Churchill’s warning and hindsight

Critics such as Churchill warned that each concession could encourage Hitler to demand more. After March 1939, earlier reassurances were much harder to defend.

A balanced judgement

Ask which evidence is strongest: short-term avoidance of war versus weakening deterrence and sacrificing smaller states. Explain why the answer depends partly on the information available in 1936–38.

Interpretation D · Lord Halifax recalling events in a 1957 memoir
“I have little doubt that if we had then told Hitler bluntly to go back, his power for future and larger mischief would have been broken. But there was no section of British public opinion that would not have been directly opposed to such action in 1936. To go to war with Germany for walking into their own backyard, which was how the British people saw it, at a time moreover when you were actually discussing with them the dates and conditions of their right to resume occupation, was not the sort of thing people could understand. So that moment which offered the last effective chance of securing peace without war, went by.”

Analyse provenance / usefulness: Halifax’s retrospective view contains both a criticism of lost opportunity and a defence of contemporary political constraints.

Grade 8–9 exam skill: Explain the link between the event, the response of other powers and the consequence for the balance of power. For any source, consider its origin, audience, purpose and what contextual knowledge confirms or challenges it.

8.1 · Source inference

What can you infer from Source B (German troops greeted in the Rhineland) about the reaction to remilitarisation? Use the source and your contextual knowledge.

4 marks
Writing guidance (no model answer)

Identify one inference and support it with visible detail. Avoid claiming the photograph proves every German approved.

Reception of troops by civilians; soldiers marching without opposition; limits of a staged/selected photograph.
8.3 · Write an account

Write an account of how Hitler achieved Anschluss with Austria between 1934 and March 1938.

8 marks
Writing guidance (no model answer)

Organise chronologically: 1934 failure → Italian shift → pressure on Schuschnigg → resignation → 12 March invasion. Explain the links.

Dollfuss coup failed; Mussolini changed stance; February Berchtesgaden intimidation; cancelled plebiscite; Seyss-Inquart; March 1938 troops.
8.5 · Sources usefulness

How useful are the Italian propaganda illustration (Source B, 8.5) and Hitler’s Berlin speech (Source C, 8.5) to a historian studying the Sudeten Crisis?

12 marks
Writing guidance (no model answer)

Evaluate both sources separately for content, provenance, purpose, limitations and contextual knowledge. Reach a comparative conclusion.

Italian visual presentation; possible pro-German bias; Hitler’s public assurance versus eventual occupation of Prague; audience/purpose and factual context.
8.6 · Write an account

Write an account of the events that led to the Munich Agreement in September 1938 and its immediate consequences.

8 marks
Writing guidance (no model answer)

Use precise dates and links: Sudeten demands → Berchtesgaden → Bad Godesberg → Munich → loss of Czech defences.

September talks; escalating demands; Germany Britain France Italy; Czech exclusion; Sudetenland transfer; military and political consequences.
8.8A · Sources usefulness

How useful is the Daily Express extract of 30 September 1938 to a historian studying why appeasement was popular in Britain?

12 marks
Writing guidance (no model answer)

Analyse both what it says and why a newspaper would write it, plus contextual evidence and limitations.

Fear of war and family safety; warm reception; newspaper’s editorial perspective; cannot represent all opinions or predict a lasting peace.
8.8B · Extended judgement

“Appeasement was a mistake that led to the outbreak of the Second World War.” How far do you agree?

16 marks + 4 SPaG
Writing guidance (no model answer)

Make a clear judgement supported by both sides. Develop 3–4 paragraphs with precise evidence and consider what leaders could know at the time.

For: emboldened Hitler; sacrificed Czechoslovakia; undermined deterrence and USSR ties. Against: public fear, France/Britain military readiness, time for rearmament, 1938 alternatives. Overall reasoned judgement.
8.7 · Consequences

Write an account of how Britain moved from appeasement in 1938 towards guaranteeing Polish independence in 1939.

8 marks
Writing guidance (no model answer)

Explain the change, not just a list of events.

Munich concessions; March 1939 Prague occupation showed aims went beyond ethnic Germans; increased doubts about Hitler; Polish guarantee.
